description: The pH scale, neutralization, buffers, and strong versus weak acids.

questions.explain: The pH scale runs 0-14: below 7 is acidic (lower = stronger), 7 is neutral, and above 7 is basic.
questions.q: A solution with a pH of 3 is best described as what?

questions.explain: Arrhenius acids increase H+ (which forms hydronium in water); Arrhenius bases increase OH- (hydroxide) instead.
questions.q: An Arrhenius acid is a substance that releases which ion in water?

questions.explain: Neutralization: H+ from the acid joins OH- from the base to make water, and the leftover ions form a salt.
questions.q: When an acid and a base neutralize each other, the products are what?

questions.explain: The pH scale is logarithmic: 7 minus 2 = 5 pH units, so 10^5 = 100,000 times more acidic.
questions.q: Lemon juice (pH about 2) is how many times more acidic than pure water (pH 7)?

questions.explain: Ammonia solution is basic (around pH 11) and is a common glass-cleaner ingredient. Vinegar, citric acid, and carbonic acid are all acids.
questions.q: Which of these is a common base found in household products?

questions.explain: Buffers mop up added H+ or OH- so pH stays stable - blood buffers hold human blood near pH 7.4 despite everything we eat and do.
options: Instantly neutralizes any amount of acid
questions.q: A buffer solution is valuable because it does what?

questions.explain: Litmus rules: blue litmus turns red in acid, and red litmus turns blue in base. Phenolphthalein, by contrast, turns pink in bases, not acids.
questions.q: Which indicator change signals an acidic solution?

questions.explain: Blood is slightly basic, held near 7.4 by buffers. Deviations of even a few tenths can be dangerous.
questions.q: Normal human blood has a pH of about what?

questions.explain: Strength is about ionization: HCl is strong because it dissociates fully; acetic acid is weak because most molecules stay intact. Strength is not the same as concentration.
options: It has a higher pH than weak acids
It ionizes (dissociates) almost completely in water
It tastes more sour than a weak acid
It cannot be neutralized by a base
questions.q: A strong acid differs from a weak acid because a strong acid does what?

questions.explain: Antacids contain mild bases like calcium carbonate that react with and neutralize excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach.

Slow down acid production for a full day
questions.q: Antacid tablets relieve heartburn mainly by doing what?

It stores data in a variable

until the user closes the program

A loop with no code inside it

description: What endodontists, periodontists, orthodontists, and the other recognized specialists actually do.

questions.explain: Endodontics focuses on the tooth's interior: root canal therapy, retreatments, and apicoectomy surgery on the root tip.
questions.q: Which dental specialist focuses on root canal therapy?

questions.explain: Periodontics covers the gums and supporting bone: treating gum disease, scaling and root planing, bone grafts, and placing implants.
questions.q: A periodontist specializes in what?

questions.explain: Orthodontists diagnose and correct malocclusion - crooked teeth, bite problems, and jaw growth - using braces, aligners, and other appliances.
options: Correcting malocclusion and aligning the teeth and jaws
questions.q: An orthodontist's primary focus is what?

questions.explain: Pediatric dentists (pedodontists) treat infants through adolescents, combining dentistry with behavior guidance and preventive care for young patients.
questions.q: Which specialist would most often treat a 4-year-old with extensive decay?

questions.explain: Prosthodontics is the restoration and replacement of teeth: crowns, bridges, veneers, implants, and full or partial dentures.
options: Replacing missing teeth with crowns, bridges, implants, and dentures
questions.q: A prosthodontist specializes in what?

questions.explain: Oral and maxillofacial surgeons handle extractions (including impacted wisdom teeth), corrective jaw surgery, trauma repair, and implant placement.
options: Surgical removal of impacted third molars (wisdom teeth)
questions.q: An oral and maxillofacial surgeon would perform which procedure?

questions.explain: Oral pathologists are the diagnosticians of dentistry: they examine biopsied tissue under a microscope to identify oral diseases and cancers.
options: Diagnose diseases of the oral cavity by examining biopsy tissue
questions.q: An oral pathologist's primary role is what?

questions.explain: Bone grafting, guided tissue regeneration, and treating advanced bone loss are periodontal surgical procedures.
questions.q: A patient with severe gum recession and bone loss needing a bone graft is referred to which specialist?

questions.explain: Oral and maxillofacial radiology is the specialty devoted to interpreting advanced imaging, from CBCT scans to complex diagnoses of jaw pathology.
questions.q: Which specialty centers on interpreting advanced dental imaging, such as CBCT scans for complex diagnoses?

questions.explain: Dental public health works at the population level: water fluoridation, school sealant and screening programs, access-to-care initiatives, and health education.
options: Community prevention programs like water fluoridation and school sealant programs
questions.q: Dental public health specialists focus on what kind of work?

subject: Dental Fundamentals
title: Dental Specialties

description: Four-handed dentistry, instrument transfer, suctioning, and moisture control.

questions.explain: Four-handed dentistry frees the operator to stay focused: the assistant keeps the field visible and dry with suction and retraction while passing instruments on cue.
options: Keep the field visible and dry, transfer instruments, and retract tissue
Take the final impression without help
Adjust the chair and leave the room
questions.q: In four-handed dentistry, the dental assistant's main role is to do what?

questions.explain: The HVE tip belongs at the operative site with its bevel parallel to the tooth surface, placed before the handpiece starts, to capture spray and debris at the source.
options: Close to the tooth being treated, with the bevel parallel to the tooth surface
Only in the back of the mouth
questions.q: Where should the high-volume evacuator (HVE) tip be positioned?

questions.explain: For a right-handed operator: the operator's zone is 7 to 12 o'clock, the assistant's zone is 2 to 4, the transfer zone is 4 to 7, and the static zone is 12 to 2.
questions.q: For a right-handed dentist, the operator's working zone is which area?

questions.explain: Deliver the instrument handle-first with its working end already oriented for the arch being treated, so the dentist can use it immediately without repositioning.
options: Handle first, with the working end pointing anywhere
With the working end pointing toward the assistant
Only when the dentist looks up from the patient
With the working end positioned for use on the correct arch
questions.q: When transferring an instrument, the assistant should deliver it how?

questions.explain: The saliva ejector is low-volume - fine for saliva control but unable to keep up with handpiece spray. The HVE is the tool for moisture control during active treatment.
options: To remove small amounts of saliva and fluids for patient comfort (low-volume suction)
To replace the HVE during restorative work
To dry a tooth for bonding
questions.q: What is the purpose of the saliva ejector?

questions.explain: Trays are laid out in the sequence the instruments will be needed, so transfer is automatic and the operator never waits.
options: In the order of use, from left to right
Randomly, as long as everything is present
questions.q: Instruments on a preset tray should be arranged in what order?

questions.explain: The dental dam gives the best isolation, retracts the cheeks and tongue, and protects the airway; cotton rolls and dry angles are quicker but less complete alternatives.
questions.q: Which moisture-control method uses a thin sheet to isolate a single tooth or quadrant?

questions.explain: The transfer zone is over the patient's chest in the 4 to 7 o'clock area. Never pass instruments over the patient's face.
options: Over the patient's chest, below the chin area (4 to 7 o'clock)
Above the head of the chair
questions.q: The instrument transfer zone is located where?

questions.explain: Maxillary (upper) work gets the working end pointed up; mandibular (lower) work gets it pointed down - matched to the arch so no adjustment is needed.
options: Down, toward the mandibular arch in use
questions.q: When the dentist is working on a mandibular (lower) tooth, instruments are delivered with the working end pointing which way?

questions.explain: The assistant sits slightly higher (eyes about 4-6 inches above the operator's eye level) to see into the mouth clearly and reach the oral cavity without leaning over the patient.
options: At exactly the same height as the dentist
Slightly higher than the dentist (eyes 4-6 inches above the operator's eye level)
questions.q: For proper four-handed dentistry, the chairside assistant sits how?

description: Identify nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, and interjections in context.

questions.explain: Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs, and often (but not always) end in -ly. "Swiftly" describes how the dog ran, so it modifies the verb "ran."
questions.q: In the sentence "The quick dog ran swiftly," which word is the adverb?

questions.explain: A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea. "Happiness" is an abstract idea functioning as the sentence's subject, so it is a noun.
questions.q: In "Happiness filled the room," what part of speech is "happiness"?

questions.explain: Adverbs can modify adjectives, not just verbs. "Extremely" describes the degree of tiredness, so it modifies the adjective "tired."
questions.q: In "She is extremely tired," what part of speech is "extremely"?

questions.explain: A preposition shows the relationship between a noun or pronoun and other words in the sentence. "To" links "store" to the verb phrase, showing direction.
questions.q: In "They walked to the store," what part of speech is "to"?

questions.explain: Interjections are exclamations that express strong emotion and stand apart from the sentence's grammar. "Wow!" shows sudden feeling, while the others are a verb, an adjective, and a preposition.
questions.q: Which of these words is an interjection?

questions.explain: Both "quickly" and "unanimously" describe how the members voted, so both modify the verb "voted" — making both adverbs.
questions.q: In "The committee members voted quickly and unanimously," which words are the adverbs?

questions.explain: Conjunctions join words, phrases, or clauses. Coordinating conjunctions — and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet (FANBOYS) — join grammatically equal elements.
questions.q: What part of speech connects two clauses, as "and" does in "I like tea, and she likes coffee"?

questions.explain: "Dramatically" describes the manner of the improvement — how the writing improved — so it modifies the verb "improved."
questions.q: In "Her writing improved dramatically," what does "dramatically" modify?

questions.explain: When "well" follows a linking verb and describes the subject's state (health or condition), it acts as a predicate adjective. In the other sentences it modifies verbs, making it an adverb.
options: She did well on the exam.
questions.q: Which sentence uses "well" as an adjective rather than an adverb?

questions.explain: Correlative conjunctions are pairs that work together — either/or, neither/nor, both/and, not only/but also — and must be followed by parallel grammatical structures.
questions.q: In "Either you come with us, or you stay here," what part of speech are "either" and "or"?

subject: English & Grammar
title: Parts of Speech

description: Master commas, semicolons, colons, apostrophes, hyphens, and quotation marks.

questions.explain: A semicolon joins two closely related INDEPENDENT clauses. "I studied for weeks" could stand alone as a sentence. Never put a semicolon before a conjunction like "and," and never use one to separate a fragment.
options: The test was hard; I studied for weeks.
My favorite colors; are blue and green.
She ran fast; and won the race.
questions.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?

questions.explain: For irregular plural nouns that do not end in s — children, men, women — form the possessive by adding 's: "the children's toys."
questions.q: Where does the apostrophe go in the possessive of "children"?

questions.explain: In a series of three or more items, place a comma between each item. The Oxford (serial) comma before "and" is standard in formal American writing and prevents ambiguity.
options: Bring a pencil, eraser, and notebook.
Bring a pencil, eraser and, notebook.
Bring, a pencil, eraser, and notebook.
Bring a pencil eraser, and notebook.
questions.q: Which sentence punctuates a list correctly?

questions.explain: A colon must follow a COMPLETE independent clause, and it introduces something that explains or expands on it — a list, a quote, or a clarification.
options: Before any list, even a fragment
To introduce a list, explanation, or quote after a complete clause
Anywhere you would use a period
questions.q: When should you use a colon?

questions.explain: In American English, periods and commas always go INSIDE the closing quotation mark. "She said 'Hello.'" is correct; the period must not sit outside the quotes.
questions.q: Which quotation is punctuated correctly in American English?

questions.explain: Nonrestrictive (nonessential) clauses add extra information and are set off by commas. "Who lives in Denver" can be removed without changing the core meaning, so it takes commas.
options: My brother, who lives in Denver, is visiting.
My brother who lives in Denver is visiting.
The car which is red, is very fast.
questions.q: Which sentence uses commas around a nonrestrictive clause correctly?

questions.explain: A run-on fuses two independent clauses with no punctuation, or with only a comma (a comma splice). Fix it by splitting with a period or semicolon, or by joining with a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS).
options: Adding more commas wherever it feels long
Using a semicolon or period to split the clauses, or adding a coordinating conjunction
questions.q: A run-on sentence is best fixed by which method?

questions.explain: For plural nouns ending in s, add only an apostrophe: "the companies' profits." The singular possessive is "the company's profits."
questions.q: Which is the correct plural possessive of "companies"?

questions.explain: Compound adjectives BEFORE a noun are hyphenated: "a well-known author." After the noun, no hyphen is needed: "The author is well known."
options: The author is well - known for her books.
questions.q: Which sentence uses a hyphen correctly?

questions.explain: Use a comma after an introductory phrase or clause. "After the storm" sets up the sentence but is not the main clause, so the comma separates it from "we cleaned the yard."
options: It separates the subject from the verb
questions.q: In "After the storm, we cleaned the yard," why is the comma after "storm" correct?

subject: English & Grammar
title: Punctuation Rules

description: Fix the mistakes everyone makes: their/they're, affect/effect, pronoun cases, and agreement.

questions.explain: They're = they are (a contraction). Their = possessive. There = a place. Only "They're going" expands to "They are going," which is correct here.
options: Their going to the store later.
They're going to loose the game.
There going to win for sure.
They're going to the store later.
questions.q: Choose the correct sentence:

questions.explain: Affect is usually the VERB meaning to influence: "will affect morale." Effect is usually the NOUN meaning a result: "the effect was positive."
options: The new policy will affect morale.
The affect of the storm was severe.
The medicine will effect you strongly.
questions.q: Which sentence uses "affect" and "effect" correctly?

questions.explain: In the subject position, use subject pronouns: "He and I went." Test by removing the other person — "He went to lunch" works, but "Him went" and "Me went" do not.
options: Me and him went to lunch.
Him and I went to lunch.
He and I went to lunch.
Him and me went to lunch.
questions.q: Which sentence uses subject pronouns correctly?

questions.explain: Ignore prepositional phrases ("of students," "on the shelf") when finding the true subject. "Committee" is singular here, so it takes "meets" — and "news" is singular despite ending in s.
options: The group of students are studying.
The books on the shelf is dusty.
questions.q: Choose the sentence with correct subject-verb agreement:

questions.explain: Use "fewer" for countable nouns (people, apples) and "less" for uncountable quantities (water, milk, time). "Fewer people" is correct.
options: There is fewer water in the glass.
There are fewer people in line today.
I have less apples than you do.
Fewer milk is left in the fridge.
questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses "fewer" vs. "less"?

questions.explain: The participial phrase "driving to work" attaches to "deer," implying the deer was driving. Place the modifier next to the word it describes: "Driving to work, I saw a deer."
options: Running late, the bus left without me.
Covered in mud, the dog needed a bath.
Tired and hungry, we ate dinner.
I saw a deer driving to work.
questions.q: Which sentence contains a misplaced modifier?

questions.explain: Parallel structure requires items in a series to share the same grammatical form. All three gerunds — hiking, swimming, biking — match.
options: She likes hiking, swimming, and biking.
She likes hiking, swimming, and to bike.
She likes to hike, swimming, and biking.
She likes hiking, to swim, and biking.
questions.q: Which sentence uses parallel structure correctly?

questions.explain: Prepositions take OBJECT pronouns: "between you and ME." Test by dropping the other person — "between me" works, but "between I" never does.
options: The sentence needs a comma after "I".
The sentence should end with a question mark.
questions.q: "Between you and I, this test is hard." What is wrong?

questions.explain: "Could of" is a mishearing of the contraction "could've" (could HAVE). Always write "could have," "should have," or "would have" — never "of."
questions.q: Which sentence spells the contraction correctly?

questions.explain: Two negatives cancel into a positive in standard English. "Don't need any help" uses one negative with "any" — the correct pattern. The others accidentally say the opposite of what is intended.
questions.q: Which sentence avoids a double negative?

subject: English & Grammar
title: Common Errors

description: Subjects, predicates, objects, clauses, and the four sentence types.

questions.explain: A complete sentence needs a subject, a predicate (verb), and a complete thought. Only "The dog barked loudly" has all three; the others are fragments.
questions.q: Which is a complete sentence?

questions.explain: The predicate is everything the subject DOES — the verb plus its objects and modifiers. "Answered the question" is the complete predicate; "answered" alone is the simple predicate.
questions.q: What is the predicate in "The tall student answered the question"?

questions.explain: A compound sentence joins TWO or more independent clauses, usually with a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS). "The movie was long" and "the ending was great" could each stand alone.
options: I went home after the game ended.
The movie was long, but the ending was great.
Running every morning, she stayed fit.
The cat that I adopted sleeps all day.
questions.q: Which sentence is a compound sentence?

questions.explain: A complex sentence has one independent clause ("we played anyway") plus at least one dependent clause ("Although it rained," which cannot stand alone).
questions.q: Identify the sentence type: "Although it rained, we played anyway."

questions.explain: "Walking to the store yesterday" is a participial phrase with no subject or finite verb — it cannot stand alone. Add both: "She was walking to the store yesterday."
questions.q: Which is a sentence fragment?

questions.explain: The direct object receives the action of the verb and answers "what?" — She threw WHAT? "The ball." It follows an action verb.
questions.q: What is the direct object in "She threw the ball"?

questions.explain: "When the bell rang" has a subject and verb, but the subordinating conjunction "when" makes it unable to stand alone — that is what makes it a dependent (subordinate) clause.
options: When the bell rang, the students left.
questions.q: Which sentence contains a dependent clause?

questions.explain: The indirect object answers "to whom" or "for whom" — the teacher gave homework TO the students. The direct object (homework) receives the action; the indirect object receives the direct object.
questions.q: "The teacher gave the students homework." What is "the students"?

questions.explain: The first is a comma splice, the fourth is a run-on, and a semicolon cannot precede a conjunction. The subordinating conjunction "because" correctly shows the cause-and-effect relationship in one complex sentence.
options: It was raining, we stayed inside.
It was raining; and we stayed inside.
Because it was raining, we stayed inside.
It was raining we stayed inside.
questions.q: Which correctly combines these sentences: "It was raining. We stayed inside."?

questions.explain: A simple sentence has exactly one independent clause — one subject-predicate pair expressing a complete thought. "Simple" refers to structure, not length; a simple sentence can still be long.
options: One independent and one dependent clause
questions.q: A simple sentence contains:

Pharmacology Basics
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: Medication rights, routes, safety checks, and common drug facts every nurse must know.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the traditional five rights of medication administration?
questions.explain: The five rights are right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, and right time. The diagnosis guides prescribing but is not one of the administration rights — right documentation is often added as the sixth right.

questions.q: A nurse sees an order for Tylenol. What is the generic name the pharmacy will dispense?
questions.explain: Tylenol is the brand name for acetaminophen. Nurses should know generics because orders, labels, and references often list them — and mixing up names (e.g., aspirin vs. acetaminophen) causes real errors.

questions.q: Which medication route provides the fastest onset of action?
questions.explain: IV drugs enter the bloodstream immediately, so onset is nearly instant. Sublingual is fast but slower than IV; oral is the slowest because the drug must survive digestion and first-pass metabolism in the liver.

questions.q: A patient shows signs of anaphylaxis after a new medication. The nurse's first-line treatment is:
questions.explain: Epinephrine IM into the lateral thigh is the first-line treatment — it reverses airway swelling and restores blood pressure in minutes. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts, never substitutes.

questions.q: Before administering digoxin, the nurse must assess the:
options: Apical pulse for one full minute
questions.explain: Digoxin slows the heart; the apical pulse must be counted for a full minute and the dose held (and the provider notified) if the rate is below 60 bpm in adults. A wrist pulse is not accurate enough.

questions.q: Which abbreviation is on the official 'Do Not Use' list because it is easily misread?
questions.explain: 'QD' has been misread as 'QID' (four times daily), causing overdoses. It must be written as 'daily.' Trailing zeros (1.0 mg), 'U' for units, and MSO4/MgSO4 are also banned.

questions.q: Peak and trough drug levels are routinely monitored for which medication?
questions.explain: Vancomycin (and aminoglycosides like gentamicin) have a narrow therapeutic window — too little fails to kill bacteria, too much damages kidneys and hearing. Troughs are drawn just before the next dose.

questions.q: A patient on warfarin is bleeding. The specific antidote the nurse should anticipate is:
questions.explain: Vitamin K reverses warfarin's anticoagulant effect; in life-threatening bleeding, fresh frozen plasma or PCC is also given. Protamine sulfate reverses heparin, and naloxone reverses opioids — know the pairing for each drug class.

questions.q: Which drug is an opioid antagonist used to reverse opioid overdose?
questions.explain: Naloxone displaces opioids from receptors and can restore breathing within minutes. Because its effect is shorter than most opioids, patients must still be monitored for re-sedation.

questions.q: A patient asks to crush their enteric-coated tablet because it is hard to swallow. The nurse should:
options: Crush it and mix with applesauce
Tell the patient to swallow it whole and contact the provider for an alternative
questions.explain: Enteric coating protects the stomach from the drug (or the drug from stomach acid); crushing destroys that protection and can cause harm. Never crush enteric-coated, extended-release, or sublingual medications — request an alternative formulation instead.

title: Vital Signs & Assessment
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: Measuring and interpreting temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and pain.

questions.q: According to current guidelines, a normal blood pressure for an adult is:
questions.explain: The AHA defines normal as below 120/80. Readings of 120-129/<80 are 'elevated,' and 130/80 or higher is hypertension — these thresholds guide when treatment begins.

questions.q: Which temperature site is considered the most accurate reflection of core body temperature?
questions.explain: Rectal readings most closely reflect core temperature, though they are invasive. Axillary runs about a degree lower and is the least accurate; oral and temporal are practical compromises.

questions.q: Tachycardia in an adult is defined as a heart rate above:
questions.explain: Above 100 bpm at rest is tachycardia; below 60 is bradycardia. Context matters — fever, pain, anxiety, and exercise all raise the rate, so trend the numbers, not just one reading.

questions.q: When assessing respirations, the best nursing practice is to:
options: Announce you are counting breaths and count for 15 seconds
Count for 30 seconds right after telling the patient
Count during conversation for one minute
Count for a full minute after taking the pulse, without the patient knowing
questions.explain: People unconsciously change their breathing when they know it's being watched. Counting for a full minute after the pulse keeps the patient unaware and catches irregular patterns a 15-second count would miss.

questions.q: A normal pulse oximetry (SpO2) reading for a healthy adult is:
questions.explain: 95-100% is normal; below 90% generally requires intervention. Remember that oximetry measures saturation, not ventilation — a patient can have a normal SpO2 and still be in trouble, so assess breathing, not just the number.

questions.q: Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a systolic drop of at least ___ within 3 minutes of standing:
questions.explain: A drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic (with symptoms like dizziness) within 3 minutes of standing defines orthostatic hypotension. It signals fall risk — sit the patient back down and notify the provider.

questions.q: Using a blood pressure cuff that is too small for the patient's arm will produce a reading that is:
questions.explain: A cuff that's too narrow needs extra pressure to compress the artery, inflating the reading. The bladder should encircle about 80% of the arm — when in doubt, use the larger cuff.

questions.q: Pain is frequently referred to as the:
questions.explain: Pain is called the fifth vital sign because it must be assessed with every set of vitals. It's the one subjective sign — measured by the patient's report, often on a 0-10 scale.

questions.q: The apical pulse is best auscultated at which location?
options: 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line
questions.explain: The apex of the heart sits at the 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line (point of maximal impulse). This is the true ventricular rate — always use it for irregular rhythms and before digoxin.

questions.q: A temperature above ___ is generally considered a fever (pyrexia) in adults:
questions.explain: 100.4 F (38 C) or higher is the standard fever threshold. Report fevers promptly — they can signal infection, transfusion reactions, or other complications, especially in postoperative or immunocompromised patients.

title: Patient Safety
subject: Nursing Fundamentals
description: Fall prevention, restraints, sentinel events, and keeping patients safe.

questions.q: Immediately after a patient falls, the nurse's first action should be to:
options: Help the patient back to bed
questions.explain: Assessment always comes first — a fall can cause fractures, head injury, or bleeding that must be found before anything else. The provider call and incident report follow, and the fall gets documented in the chart.

questions.q: Before applying physical restraints, the nurse is required to first:
options: Document the need in the chart
questions.explain: Restraints are a last resort: federal rules and nursing ethics require trying alternatives first (reorientation, family presence, toileting, pain control). Restraints need a provider order, time limits, and frequent monitoring.

questions.q: Which patient is at the highest risk for a fall?
options: A 30-year-old on postoperative day 3, walking with help
A 45-year-old with a peripheral IV, resting in bed
A 78-year-old on a sedative and a diuretic
questions.explain: Fall risk multiplies with age, altered mentation, and medications — sedatives impair balance and diuretics cause urgency and orthostatic drops. Screen every patient with a fall-risk tool and act on the score.

questions.q: The surgical 'time out' immediately before an incision verifies the:
options: Correct patient, correct site, and correct procedure
questions.explain: The whole team pauses to confirm identity, site (with marking), and procedure aloud. It was created specifically to eliminate wrong-patient, wrong-site, wrong-procedure surgery — a classic sentinel event.

questions.q: Keeping the bed in its lowest position with the call light in reach is an example of:
questions.explain: Low bed, locked brakes, call light within reach, and hourly rounding are the core fall-prevention bundle. They're simple, evidence-based, and required by most hospital policies.

questions.q: A medication error is caught before reaching the patient (a near miss). The nurse should:
options: Ignore it since no harm occurred
Document it only in the patient's chart
Tell the patient what almost happened
questions.explain: Near misses are reported through the incident system so the process flaw can be fixed before someone is harmed. Incident reports are quality-improvement tools — they do not go in the patient's chart and are not for punishment.

questions.q: Using the RACE fire-response sequence, the nurse's first action is to:
questions.explain: RACE = Rescue, Alarm, Confine, Extinguish. People come first — move anyone in immediate danger, then pull the alarm, close doors to contain smoke and fire, and only then attempt to extinguish if trained.

questions.q: Which of the following is classified as a sentinel event?
questions.explain: A sentinel event is an unexpected occurrence involving death or serious harm — wrong-site surgery is the textbook example. Sentinel events trigger root-cause analysis and must be reported to The Joint Commission.

questions.q: Raising all four side rails on a patient's bed may be considered:
questions.explain: Four raised rails can trap a patient in bed and are treated as a restraint under many facility policies — requiring assessment, orders, and monitoring. Two or fewer rails for positioning is generally not a restraint.

questions.q: The primary purpose of filing an incident report is:
options: To document the event in the patient's medical record
To inform the patient of the error
questions.explain: Incident reports identify system problems so they can be fixed — they exist for quality improvement, not blame. They are internal risk-management documents and are never filed in the patient's chart.

description: Thresholds, vision, hearing, pain, and how the brain organizes sensory input.

questions.explain: Sensation is the raw detection of physical energy by sensory receptors (light hitting the retina). Perception is the brain's active organization and interpretation of that input into meaningful experience.
options: Sensation is conscious; perception is unconscious.
They are the same process with different names.
Sensation involves memory; perception does not.
Sensation is detecting stimuli; perception is organizing and interpreting them.
questions.q: What is the difference between sensation and perception?

questions.explain: The absolute threshold is the minimum stimulation needed for detection 50% of the time — classically, a candle flame seen 30 miles away on a dark, clear night. "Smallest noticeable difference" describes the DIFFERENCE threshold instead.
options: The maximum stimulus we can tolerate
The point where sensation becomes perception
The minimum stimulus intensity detected 50% of the time
The smallest noticeable difference between stimuli
questions.q: The absolute threshold is defined as:

questions.explain: Weber's law: the just noticeable difference (JND) is a constant PROPORTION of the original stimulus. You would notice 1 lb added to 10 lbs, but need about 10 lbs added to 100 lbs to notice — the ratio stays constant.
options: The just noticeable difference is a constant proportion of the original stimulus
Sensation grows linearly with stimulus intensity
Thresholds are identical across all senses
questions.q: Weber's law states that:

questions.explain: In the famous Simons and Chabris study, viewers counting basketball passes failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene — focused attention makes us blind to unexpected stimuli.
options: Failing to notice a gorilla in a basketball-passing video
questions.q: Inattentional blindness is best demonstrated by:

questions.explain: The retina lines the back of the eye and holds the photoreceptors: rods (dim light, peripheral vision) and cones (color, fine detail). The cornea and lens only focus light; the optic nerve carries the signal out.
questions.q: Which structure contains the photoreceptors (rods and cones)?

questions.explain: Trichromatic theory holds that three cone types — sensitive to short (blue), medium (green), and long (red) wavelengths — combine their signals to produce all color experience. It explains color mixing but not afterimages; that's opponent-process theory.
options: Three types of cones sensitive to red, green, and blue wavelengths
Opponent processes located in the thalamus
A single cone type that adapts to light
questions.q: The Young-Helmholtz trichromatic theory explains color vision by:

questions.explain: Gate-control theory (Melzack and Wall) says non-pain signals can close spinal "gates" to pain input — which is why rubbing a bumped elbow reduces pain, and why distraction and placebos can modulate pain.
options: Pain signals can be blocked by neural "gates" in the spinal cord
questions.q: The gate-control theory of pain proposes that:

questions.explain: Bottom-up (data-driven) processing builds perception from sensory details upward — for example, assembling lines and curves into the letter A. Top-down processing instead applies expectations and prior knowledge downward onto the input.
options: Building perception from raw sensory input upward
Processing that always starts in the cortex
questions.q: Bottom-up processing is:
